description: We’re Team ASTRION from Paraguay. We bring together visual design, storytelling, and game development to create a first hands-on STEM experience for children. In ASTRION, players build a spacecraft and learn by testing their ideas. If you’re interested in making space science accessible and have skills in game development, STEM education, or astronomy, we’d love to work with you.
summary:
ASTRION is a web game for kids aged 9 to 12 that turns space mission design into play. Players build their own Earth observation satellite by choosing between real trade-offs: a sharper camera uses more battery, a bigger battery adds mass, a larger antenna sends more data but costs energy, and everything must fit in the rocket. A pre-flight check shows whether their design will work. Then the satellite flies over a real map of Paraguay, takes two photos of the Gran Chaco forest, faces a random problem (clouds, a shaky camera or a weak signal), passes through Earth's shadow and sends its data to a ground station. Finally, players compare real NASA Landsat images of the same place in 1985 and today and discover the deforestation with their own eyes.

ASTRION addresses the challenge by letting kids experience the full mission cycle: design, test, fly and discover. It matters because it shows them, with real NASA data from their own region, how satellites help us understand and protect our planet.
details:
What it does and how it works

ASTRION guides kids through a complete, simplified space mission in five steps:

1. Build the satellite. In a workshop, players drag parts onto their satellite: camera, solar panels, battery and antenna. Each part has two options with real trade-offs in energy, mass, budget and data capacity.

2. Pre-flight check. Before launch, the game runs the mission with the same rules as the flight and says, in plain words, whether energy, photo sending and the rocket are enough. If not, it takes the player straight to the part to change.

3. Fly over the Chaco. The satellite flies by itself over a real map of Paraguay. It takes two photos of the Gran Chaco forest, from 1985 and from today, passes through Earth's shadow (no solar recharge), faces one random problem (clouds, a shaky camera or a weak signal) that costs energy to fix, and sends its photos to a ground station in Asunción. A small antenna may not send everything.

4. Investigate. A lens over today's Landsat image shows the same place in 1985. Players find two changes and answer what happened to the forest.

5. Results. Players see what they practiced: designing, testing, discovering. If something failed, the game explains what was missing and invites them to improve their design.

Benefits and intended impact

Kids learn how engineers design missions: every part solves something and costs something, and there is no single right answer. They learn how an Earth observation satellite works (energy, shadow, data link) and how comparing satellite images reveals environmental change. Using a real case from Paraguay, deforestation in the Gran Chaco, connects space science to their own region and shows why satellite data matters for protecting the planet. Failing is part of the game: a failed mission explains why and invites another try.

Tools and technologies

- JavaScript, with Phaser 4 for the game scenes and Vite for development and builds.

- Three.js for the rotating 3D Earth and MapLibre GL JS for the map of Paraguay.

- Web Audio API for sound effects; ElevenLabs for the recorded voice of NOAH, the ship's AI guide.

- Game rules in plain JavaScript, covered by automated tests (node --test).

- NASA data: Landsat images (NASA SVS, ID 15026), NASA GIBS Blue Marble and Blue Marble Next Generation; Natural Earth for borders.

- Published as a free web app on GitHub Pages: no installation, no accounts.

How it is creative

- The satellite is built by hand, piece by piece, and the same satellite then flies the mission.

- The photos players take during the flight "render" line by line like a real satellite sensor, and the 1985 and today images appear side by side as soon as the second photo is taken.

- The investigation uses a "time lens": moving it over today's image reveals the past.

- Problems happen on the map, around the satellite, with the camera view shognal loss.

- NOAH, a voiced AI guide in Spanish, accompanies the whole mission.

Factors the team considered

- Age (9–12): one task per screen, few words, instant feedback, and a game that moves on by itself when there is nothing to decide.

- Honesty about data: NASA images are used unaltered (only cropped and resizat is simulated (the satellite, route, problems and ground station).

- Accessibility and reach: runs in any modern browser, with mouse or touch, keyboard-friendly dialogs, reduced motion respected, and no personal data collected.

- Local relevance: a mission over Paraguay, in Spanish (with the "vos" form a forest the players may know.
